---
title: "Maximum Likelihood as Orthogonal Projection"
description: "Original mathematical teaching with a worked delivery-operations example; MML §9.4."
---

**Study reference:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, §9.4. The examples, reasoning and notation explanations are written independently.

## Start from a problem

Least squares also has a geometric interpretation. The fitted prediction vector is the orthogonal projection of the observed times onto the column space of X.

## Formulate the problem mathematically

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol y}=P_X\boldsymbol y,\qquad P_X=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top,\qquad X^\top(\boldsymbol y-\hat{\boldsymbol y})=0
$$

This relation identifies the required structure. Interpret the symbols using the stated model rather than memorising the formula without its assumptions.

## Derive a worked result

For a tiny one-feature model whose column space is span((1,1)), take y=(3,1). The projection is (2,2) and the residual is (1,-1), perpendicular to (1,1). Gaussian errors with common variance make the same projection solve maximum likelihood.

## Why the mathematics matters

The displayed projector assumes full column rank; a Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse handles rank deficiency. Orthogonality of training residuals does not imply accurate extrapolation on new orders.

## Explain or calculate

Show directly that (1,-1) is orthogonal to (2,2). Why does this imply the projection cannot be improved within the span?
